claims.text: Conventional powder-metallurgy refractory high-entropy alloys typically contain higher residual oxygen levels and porosity.
3D ink extrusion followed by hydrogen de-binding and titanium-sponge-gettered vacuum sintering will reduce oxygen incorporation relative to conventional powder metallurgy.
The modified processing route will yield a denser microstructure.
The denser, lower-oxygen microstructure will form a more protective and slower-growing oxide scale.
Titanium sponge acts as an oxygen getter during vacuum sintering by preferentially reacting with residual oxygen.
Hydrogen de-binding helps remove volatile species.
3D ink extrusion produces a uniform microstructure.
Porosity and defect sites facilitate oxygen ingress.
Reduced bulk oxygen content and improved microstructural uniformity promote formation of a stable protective surface oxide.
A stable protective surface oxide slows further high-temperature oxidation.
At approximately 1200°C in air or another oxygen-rich atmosphere for 100 hours, the treated alloy will have a lower oxidation rate than the conventionally processed alloy.
The treated alloy will exhibit less oxidation-associated weight gain than the control.
The treated alloy will form a thinner oxide scale than the control.
The treated alloy will form a more adherent oxide scale than the control.
The intervention is expected to reduce oxidation rate by approximately 20–30%.
The intervention's benefit depends on the baseline alloy having significant residual oxygen or microstructural defects.
If residual oxygen and defects are already minimized by another processing method, the intervention may have negligible effect.
Alloy composition variations may change the magnitude of oxidation improvement.
